question: What are the time complexities of insertion, lookup, and deletion in `map` and `unordered_map`?

scenes.sub: Log n, guaranteed. Or constant on average, with a catch.
scenes.say: Insert, find, and erase, in map and unordered map. The numbers are easy to memorize. Knowing why is what interviewers check.

scenes.head: The whole answer in one grid
scenes.say: Map is a balanced tree, so insert, find, and erase are all O of log n, and that's guaranteed, even in the worst case. Unordered map is a hash table. Insert, find, and erase are O of one on average. But in the worst case, when keys pile into the same bucket, each one degrades to O of n. One detail: erasing a map element through an iterator you already have is amortized constant, since there's no search. That's the one grid to remember.

scenes.head: Why the worst case exists

notes.text: about one key per bucket: O(1)

scenes.say: Picture why the worst case exists. With a good hash, keys spread out, about one per bucket, so a lookup checks almost nothing. With a bad hash, or keys an attacker chose on purpose, everything lands in one bucket. Now a lookup walks a chain of n keys, and the hash table is no better than a linked list. That's why map is sometimes preferred when worst case latency really matters.

scenes.head: The costs hiding behind the big O

panels.code:
std::map<int, int> m;              // with 1,000,000 keys:
m.find(42);                        // ~20 to 40 comparisons

std::unordered_map<int, int> u;
u.reserve(1000000);                // no rehashing while filling
u.find(42);                        // hash, then check one bucket

std::unordered_map<std::string, int> s;
s.find("some long key");           // hashing a string: O(length)

scenes.say: Why log n? A balanced tree with a million keys is only about twenty to forty levels deep, so a lookup takes a few dozen comparisons. A hash lookup computes the hash, jumps to one bucket, and checks the few keys there. Two hidden costs. An insert can trigger a rehash, which is O of n, but it's rare, so inserts are still O of one on average. Calling reserve up front avoids it. And with string keys, every hash or comparison costs time proportional to the string's length.

lines: map: insert, find, erase all O(log n), guaranteed (balanced tree).
unordered_map: O(1) average, O(n) worst case when keys collide.
Rehashing is O(n) but rare. reserve() up front avoids it.
scenes.say: Map is O of log n for everything, guaranteed. Unordered map is O of one on average, but O of n in the worst case, when keys collide. Rehashing costs O of n, but it's rare, and reserve avoids it.
